newsitem.title: UK: UK's offshore oil industry faces major challenges.
newsitem.headline: UK's offshore oil industry faces major challenges.

text.p: Tuesday's budget in Britain is the latest challenge for the country's offshore oil industry, already coming to terms with the problems of decommissioning redundant installations and facing possible restrictions over working practices from the European Commission.
Chancellor Kenneth Clarke announced in his budget that he proposes to withdraw the 100 percent corporation tax deduction for the intangible costs of drilling most production oil wells.

The Treasury estimates that this measure will save 150 million stg in the tax year 1998/99, and a further 200 million stg in 1999/2000. But the industry fears that this will directly reduce the amount of money available to it for further commercial activities.

"It will impact on activity because it is taking, over a period of time, available cash flow out of the system," said George Watkins, President of industry body the U.K. Offshore Operators Association (UKOOA).
And Harold Hughes, Director General of UKOOA, added that the measure "carries some possibility of a reduction of the industry's activity level".

The budget also changes the capital allowances for "plant and machinery" with a life of more than 25 years from 25 percent to six percent. UKOOA is uncertain over what is included as "plant and machinery" -- it is not clear if this will cover pipelines, for example, or floating production vessels .
Hughes said "it is not clear yet which industry current and intended projects are intended to be affected", but the feeling is that this reduction in tax allowances may also impact on cash flow.

But the budget worries may seem marginal alongside a potential threat to working practices from the European Commission. The EC directive on working time, which limits workers in the European Union to a 48 hour week averaged over four months but also limits night shifts to a maximum eight hours, could have serious implications for the industry.

At present certain groups of workers, including offshore oil workers, are exempted from the directive. But UKOOA says "we understand that the White Paper does not contemplate continuing the exemption".

Although it is not yet certain that the industry will lose its exemption, the fear is that current working practices, with offshore workers typically working shifts of one, two or three weeks offshore followed by the same period on leave, will have to change.

UKOOA argues that workers prefer to work a long shift of 12 hours while offshore rather than working eight hours and then being "free" on a production platform for a full 16 hours, with little to do. This allows people to work a long working week of seven days of twelve hours each and then take a week off. Over a year, they work 182 days on this basis, totalling fewer hours than would be worked under the system of 48 weeks of 48 hours each, as called for in the directive.
Any change in working conditions would affect nearly 30,000 offshore workers, and UKOOA fears that it could have an impact especially on the viability of developing marginal fields.

Decommissioning of offshore installations has also come under scrutiny following a an EU report published earlier this month. This says that the majority of installations in shallow waters can be removed, and adds that complete removal and land disposal of Europe's offshore facilities would cost around 2 billion ECU ($2.56 billion) more than scrapping them according to minimum standards.
According to a UKOOA survey of its members, over the next 10 years, 50 rigs will have to be removed from the North Sea at a cost of 1.5 billion stg.

Reacting to the report, UKOOA said in a statement that it shares concerns expressed about the difficulty of removing deep water structures and adds that the industry has no experience in doing so, and that experience from the Gulf of Mexico is not transferable to the North Sea.
But UKOOA added that the report has had a substantial input from the industry.
The issue of decommissioning offshore installations came to the forefront of public opinion last year, when Shell backed down on a decision to dispose of the Brent Spar in deep water.

But UKOOA points out that of 219 installations in UK waters, some 75 percent will be removed entirely under existing regulations. The debate over disposal only applies to around 50 large steel structures and nine concrete structures which could be disposed of at sea under current regulations.
